title: Title keys with senior spelled out
prompt: Some job titles start with the short form `Sr` or `Sr.`, so senior roles are counted twice in HR's report. Write `solve(employees)` so it returns `employee_id` and a `title_key` for each employee.
rules: `title_key` is `job_title` with no spaces at the start or end, a single space between words, and all lower case.
Then, when the first word is exactly `sr` or `sr.`, it becomes `senior`: `  Sr.  Data Analyst` gives `senior data analyst`.
A title that is only the short form has no role after it and isn't expanded: `Sr` gives `sr`, ` Sr. ` gives `sr.`.
`sr` anywhere else, or as part of a longer word, stays as it is: `sre engineer` and `data analyst sr` don't change.
A missing title stays missing. Return one row per employee, with only these two columns.
hints: Tidy first, then expand: `F.lower(F.regexp_replace(F.trim("job_title"), "\\s+", " "))` gives one standard form to match against.
`^` anchors a pattern to the start, and `\.?` allows an optional dot. A dot on its own matches any character, so escape it.
Require the space after the short form, as in `^sr\.? `, and put it back in the replacement. Otherwise `sre engineer` turns into `seniore engineer`.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def solve(employees):
    # Return employee_id and title_key.
    return employees
explanation: Standardize, then rewrite. `key = F.lower(F.regexp_replace(F.trim("job_title"), "\\s+", " "))` gives one form to match against, and `F.regexp_replace(key, "^sr\\.? ", "senior ")` expands the short form. Each piece of the pattern has a job: `^` keeps it to the first word, so `data analyst sr` is left alone; `\\.?` makes the dot optional; and the space after it stops `sre` from matching. The order matters too: before `trim` and `lower`, `  SR Data Analyst` doesn't start with `sr`, so it would never match. A `replace` dict can't do this, because it only swaps whole values and would need one entry per title.
